title: Probability Distributions
summary: A random variable attaches numbers to the outcomes of a random experiment, and its probability distribution tells us how likely each value is. This chapter covers discrete random variables, expected value and variance, and the three key models used in business and science — the binomial, Poisson and normal distributions.

notes.heading: Random variables and probability distributions
notes.html:
A random variable X is a rule that assigns a real number to each outcome of a random experiment, e.g. the number of heads in three tosses, or the number of defective items in a sample. It is discrete if it takes countable values (0, 1, 2, …) and continuous if it can take any value in an interval (height, weight, time).

A probability distribution of a discrete X lists each value xi with its probability pi = P(X = xi), where every pi ≥ 0 and Σ pi = 1.

Expected value (mean): μ = E(X) = Σ xipi. Variance: σ2 = Var(X) = E(X2) − [E(X)]2 = Σ xi2pi − μ2. Standard deviation σ = √Var(X).

Rules: E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a2Var(X) (adding a constant does not change spread).

(b) A box has 10 items of which 3 are defective. Two items are drawn at random without replacement. Find the mean and variance of X = number of defective items drawn.

Total ways = 10C2 = 45. P(X = 0) = 7C2/45 = 21/45; P(X = 1) = (3 × 7)/45 = 21/45; P(X = 2) = 3C2/45 = 3/45. (Sum = 45/45 ✓.)

E(X) = 0 + 21/45 + 6/45 = 27/45 = 3/5 = 0.6. E(X2) = 21/45 + 12/45 = 33/45 = 11/15.

Var(X) = 11/15 − 9/25 = (55 − 27)/75 = 28/75 ≈ 0.373.

notes.heading: Binomial distribution
notes.html:
A Bernoulli trial has two outcomes, success (probability p) and failure (q = 1 − p). X follows a binomial distribution B(n, p) when:

  1. the number of trials n is fixed;
  2. each trial results in success or failure;
  3. the trials are independent;
  4. p is the same in every trial.

P(X = r) = nCr pr qn − r, r = 0, 1, …, n.

Mean = np, Variance = npq, SD = √(npq). Since q < 1, the variance is always less than the mean.

Worked Example 2. 10% of the bulbs made by a machine are defective. In a random sample of 5 bulbs: P(none defective) = (0.9)5 = 0.59049; P(exactly one) = 5 × 0.1 × (0.9)4 = 0.32805; P(at most one) = 0.91854; P(at least two) = 1 − 0.91854 = 0.08146. Mean = 5 × 0.1 = 0.5, variance = 5 × 0.1 × 0.9 = 0.45.

notes.heading: Poisson distribution
notes.html:
The Poisson distribution models the number of occurrences of a rare event in a fixed interval of time or space (calls per minute, accidents per day, misprints per page), when events occur independently at a constant average rate λ.

P(X = r) = e−λλr/r!, r = 0, 1, 2, …

Mean = Variance = λ.

Poisson approximation to binomial: when n is large (n ≥ 20 or so) and p is small (np ≤ 5 or so), B(n, p) ≈ Poisson with λ = np.

Useful values: e−1 ≈ 0.3679, e−2 ≈ 0.1353, e−3 ≈ 0.0498, e−4 ≈ 0.0183, e−5 ≈ 0.0067.

Worked Example 3. A helpline receives on average 2 calls per minute. P(no call in a minute) = e−2 ≈ 0.1353. P(at most 2 calls) = e−2(1 + 2 + 22/2!) = 5e−2 ≈ 0.6767. P(at least one call) = 1 − e−2 ≈ 0.8647.

notes.heading: Normal distribution
notes.html:
A continuous random variable X with mean μ and standard deviation σ is normally distributed, X ~ N(μ, σ2), when its probability curve is the bell-shaped normal curve. Properties:

  • The curve is symmetric about x = μ; mean = median = mode.
  • The total area under the curve is 1; the area to each side of μ is 0.5.
  • The curve approaches the x-axis but never touches it (asymptotic).
  • About 68.27% of values lie within μ ± σ, 95.45% within μ ± 2σ and 99.73% within μ ± 3σ.
  • Probabilities are areas: P(a < X < b) is the area under the curve between a and b.

Standard normal variable: Z = (X − μ)/σ has mean 0 and SD 1. Tables give the area from 0 to z. Values used in this chapter:

notes.heading: Worked Example 4 — normal probabilities
notes.html:
The marks of students are normally distributed with μ = 60 and σ = 8.

(a) P(X > 72): z = (72 − 60)/8 = 1.5. P(Z > 1.5) = 0.5 − 0.4332 = 0.0668.

(b) P(52 < X < 76): z1 = (52 − 60)/8 = −1, z2 = (76 − 60)/8 = 2. By symmetry, area = 0.3413 + 0.4772 = 0.8185.

(c) P(X < 56): z = −0.5. P(Z < −0.5) = 0.5 − 0.1915 = 0.3085.

(d) Marks above which the top 2.5% lie: area 0 to z = 0.4750 ⇒ z = 1.96, so x = 60 + 1.96 × 8 = 75.68.

Method: sketch the curve, shade the required region, convert to z, then add areas (opposite sides of 0) or subtract (same side).

notes.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
notes.html:
• Writing Var(X) = E(X2) − E(X) instead of E(X2) − [E(X)]2.
  • Writing Var(aX + b) = aVar(X) + b; the correct result is a2Var(X).
  • Using binomial when draws are without replacement from a small lot (trials are then not independent).
  • Forgetting that "at least one" is easiest as 1 − P(none).
  • In the Poisson distribution, saying SD = λ; it is √λ.
  • In normal problems, adding the table areas when both z values are on the same side of 0 (you must subtract).
  • Using table area as P(Z < z) directly — most tables give the area from 0 to z, so add 0.5 when needed.

questions.q: X takes values 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. Find E(X).
Find the variance of a binomial variable with n = 16 and p = 1/2.
A fair coin is tossed 5 times. Find the probability of getting exactly 3 heads.
The weekly wages of workers are normally distributed with mean ₹6,000 and SD ₹800. Find the probability that a worker earns more than ₹7,200. (Area from 0 to 1.5 = 0.4332)
A box contains 10 pens of which 3 are defective. Two pens are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability distribution of the number of defective pens drawn, and its mean and variance.

10% of the bulbs produced by a machine are defective. Find the probability that in a sample of 5 bulbs (a) none is defective, (b) at most one is defective, (c) at least two are defective. Also find the mean and variance of the number of defective bulbs.

A factory finds that 2% of its bulbs are defective. Bulbs are packed in boxes of 100. Using the Poisson distribution, find the probability that a box contains (a) no defective bulb, (b) exactly 2 defective bulbs, (c) more than 2 defective bulbs. (d) In a consignment of 1000 boxes, how many boxes are expected to contain no defective bulb? (e<sup>−2</sup> = 0.1353)
